title: Ideal gases

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Elastic collision
items.clue: Total kinetic energy is the same afterwards as before.

items.label: Real gas
items.clue: Its particles have a finite volume and attract one another.

items.label: Gas pressure
items.clue: The force per unit area exerted on the walls of a container.

questions.stem: Which statement is one of the key assumptions of the ideal gas model?

options.text: The particles lose a small amount of kinetic energy in every collision.
The spaces between the particles are filled with air that separates them.
The particles repel one another, which keeps them spread through the container.
The particles have a negligible volume compared with the volume of the gas.

questions.explanation: This is one of the model's assumptions: the particles are treated as having no volume of their own compared with the space the gas occupies. The other key assumptions are that the particles are moving, exert no intermolecular forces, and collide elastically.

questions.stem: A sample of nitrogen is held at a pressure of 2.0 × 10⁶ Pa, first at 150 K and then at 600 K. It is a gas at both temperatures. At which temperature does it deviate more from ideal gas behaviour, and why?

options.text: At 150 K, as its particles have stopped moving and so no longer collide
At 150 K, as its slower particles are affected more by the attractions between them
At 600 K, as its faster particles collide more violently with each other
At 600 K, as its particles expand when heated and take up more space

questions.explanation: At low temperature the particles have less kinetic energy, so the intermolecular attractions, which the ideal model ignores, have a significant effect on their motion. Real gases deviate most at low temperature and high pressure.

questions.stem: At STP (273.15 K, 100 kPa), 1.00 mol of helium (M = 4.00 g mol⁻¹) occupies 22.7 dm³. What volume does 1.00 mol of xenon (M = 131.29 g mol⁻¹) occupy at STP, if both behave as ideal gases?

options.text: 22.7 dm³, as heavy xenon atoms move at the same speed as the helium atoms
22.7 dm³, as volume depends only on the amount of gas at a given T and p
More than 22.7 dm³, as its much larger atoms take up more of the space
Less than 22.7 dm³, as a denser gas has its particles closer together

questions.explanation: In an ideal gas the particles have negligible volume and exert no intermolecular forces, so at a given temperature and pressure the volume depends only on the amount of gas, not on the identity or mass of the particles. 1.00 mol of xenon at STP occupies the same 22.7 dm³ as 1.00 mol of helium.

questions.stem: What volume is occupied by 0.0472 mol of an ideal gas at 30 °C and 125 kPa? R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
According to the ideal gas model, what causes the pressure that a gas exerts on the walls of its container?

options.text: Moving particles collide with the walls and exert a force on them.
The particles repel one another, so they push outwards on the walls.
The weight of the particles presses on the container, mainly on its base.
The particles expand to fill the container and press against its walls.

questions.explanation: In the model the particles move randomly and collide elastically with the walls. Each collision exerts a force on the wall; the pressure is the total force per unit area from these collisions, so it acts equally on every wall.

questions.stem: Four gases are each at 300 K and 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Which gas deviates most from ideal gas behaviour?

options.text: Helium, He, as its light atoms move the fastest and collide most violently
Neon, Ne, as its atoms are the heaviest and so they occupy the most space
Ammonia, NH₃, as hydrogen bonding attracts its molecules to one another
Methane, CH₄, as each molecule is held together by four C–H bonds

questions.explanation: Ammonia molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another, so the attractions between them are much stronger than between the particles of the other three gases. The ideal gas model assumes no intermolecular forces, so the gas with the strongest attractions deviates most.

questions.stem: What volume does 72.0 g of oxygen gas, O₂, occupy at STP (273.15 K, 100 kPa)? Molar volume of an ideal gas at STP = 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹; A_r(O) = 16.00.
A gas syringe contains 2.20 cm³ of an ideal gas at 20 °C and 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa. What amount of gas does it contain? R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
A sample of methane, CH₄, is kept at 300 K, first at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and then at 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa. It is a gas at both pressures. At which pressure does it deviate more from ideal gas behaviour, and why?

options.text: At 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa, as its particles collide more often and lose kinetic energy each time
At 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa, as its particles are close enough for their volume and attractions to matter
At 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, as its particles expand to fill the much larger volume of the gas
Neither, as at 300 K its particles move at the same average speed at both pressures

questions.stem: A fixed mass of an ideal gas is kept at constant pressure. Its volume is measured at several temperatures and plotted against temperature in °C. Which description of the graph is correct?

options.text: A straight line meeting the axis at −273 °C, where volume would be zero
A straight line meeting the axis at −273 °C, where the particles shrink to nothing
A straight line through the origin, since volume is proportional to temperature in °C
A horizontal line, as the gas fills the same container at every temperature

questions.explanation: Volume is proportional to absolute temperature. On a Celsius axis the line does not pass through the origin; extended backwards, it reaches zero volume at −273 °C (0 K), absolute zero. (A real gas would liquefy before this; the line is an extrapolation.)

questions.stem: A fixed mass of an ideal gas occupies 2.00 × 10⁻³ m³ at 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa and 27 °C. It is compressed to 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³ and at the same time its temperature rises to 87 °C. What is its new pressure?
questions.explanation: T₁ = 300 K and T₂ = 360 K. P₂ = P₁ × (V₁/V₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 1.00 × 10⁵ × 4.00 × 1.20 = 4.80 × 10⁵ Pa. The compression and the heating both raise the pressure.

questions.stem: For a fixed mass of an ideal gas at constant temperature, the pressure, p, is plotted on the y-axis against 1/V on the x-axis, where V is the volume. Which description of the graph is correct?

options.text: A straight line with a negative gradient, as p falls as 1/V rises
A curve that falls and levels off, as p and V are inversely related
A straight line through the origin, as p doubles whenever V is halved
A horizontal line, as the particles' speed and hence p do not change

questions.explanation: At constant temperature p is inversely proportional to V, so p is directly proportional to 1/V: halving V doubles 1/V and doubles p. A graph of p against 1/V is therefore a straight line through the origin.
